title: How do you prepare for online tests like McKinsey Solve and BCG Casey?
description: What to expect from online assessments that some consulting firms use before interviews, such as problem-solving games and chat-based cases, and how to…
hook: Before you reach a live case interview, many firms ask you to complete an online assessment. These can feel strange because they do not look like a normal case: some are game-like, some are written, some are chat-based. The good news is that they test the same core skills, and a little familiarity goes a long way.
body:
Common formats

  • Problem-solving games. McKinsey uses a game-based assessment called Solve. In 2026 it most often includes Redrock, a data study where you gather and analyse information to answer questions, and Sea Wolf, a simulation where you choose the right combination of options against several criteria. Some candidates also see a newer module called Sustainable Futures Lab. An older game about building an ecosystem was dropped from the standard set in 2025, so older guides may describe a test you will not see.
  • Chat-based cases. BCG uses an online case delivered by a chatbot called Casey: one business case, usually 8 to 10 questions in 25 to 30 minutes, followed by a short recorded video recommendation. Because the chatbot leads, it feels like an interviewer-led case.
  • Recorded video answers. Some firms ask you to record answers to fit or case questions with no live interviewer.
  • Numerical and logical tests. Classic timed questions on charts, data and logic.
  • Written cases. You read a pack of information and prepare slides or a short memo, then present it.

Formats change often, so always check the firm's own careers pages and any practice materials they provide. (Checked November 2026.)

How to prepare

  • Do the official practice first. Firms usually share examples. Doing them removes most of the surprise.
  • Practise chart reading and mental maths. These come up in almost every format. Try these practice questions.
  • Practise under time pressure. Most tests are timed, and pacing matters as much as accuracy.
  • Read carefully. Many mistakes come from misreading a question, not from the maths.

On the day

  • Find a quiet space, a reliable internet connection and a charged laptop.
  • Have paper, a pen and, if allowed, a calculator ready.
  • Do not get stuck on one question; if the format allows, move on and come back.

Keep it in proportion

Online tests are a gate, not the main event. Prepare enough to pass comfortably, then put most of your energy into live cases and fit stories.

Do not prepare for yesterday's test format

Online assessments can change by office, year and role. A third-party article describing a named simulation is not evidence that you will receive that simulation. Start with the actual invitation and the employer's current instructions. Confirm the duration, allowed materials, accessibility arrangements and whether there is a practice environment.

The transferable skills are stable: read the question before exploring an exhibit; track units; distinguish relevant from distracting data; and allocate time deliberately. In a fictional data task, if a product earns £12 contribution per sale and a new channel brings 4,000 incremental sales at £15,000 fixed cost, the incremental profit is £33,000 (4,000 × £12 minus £15,000). That reasoning is useful across many formats, whether the interface is a chart, simulation or spreadsheet.

Avoid treating an online assessment as a puzzle whose secret answers can be memorised. If the task prohibits outside tools or assistance, follow those rules. Afterwards, assess which fundamentals slowed you down, then train those fundamentals in normal practice rather than chasing leaked screenshots or stale module descriptions.
